recap.heading: RECAP: Session 3 : Virtualization & Hypervisors
items: 1. Virtualization Basics: Physical vs virtual resources; consolidation, isolation & utilization; types: server, storage, network, desktop, application
2. Hypervisors: Type 1 (bare-metal) vs Type 2 (hosted); Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM) & its role

sections.title: 1. Container Fundamentals: Process-level isolation; Linux namespaces & control groups (cgroups); union filesystem & layered images

slides.heading: Container Isolation Basics

content.line: A container is a running process that shares the host machine's kernel but gets its own isolated view of files, network and other processes, with no separate guest operating system of its own.
Namespaces : limit WHAT a process can see
Control groups : limit HOW MUCH it can use
Union filesystem : layers that build the image itself

slides.analogy: A large building holds many separate flats: each flat has its own rooms and lock, but all share one foundation, electricity and water line — exactly as containers share one host kernel while each gets its own isolated view through namespaces.
slides.visual_guidance: Single host kernel box at bottom; three container boxes on top, each labelled with a small lock icon and tagged Namespaces / cgroups / Union FS.

slides.heading: Linux Namespaces

content.line: A namespace isolates a process’s view of system resources, so each container gets its own view of processes, networking, and filesystems.

rows: Own filesystem view and mount points
Own user and group ID mapping

slides.visual_guidance: Six small labelled boxes around a central kernel icon, each box pointing to a different resource type from the table.

slides.heading: Cgroups And Union FS

content.line: Two more kernel features complete container isolation: control groups, known as cgroups, cap resource use, and a union filesystem builds the image itself from layers.
CPU controller: caps processor time share per group
Memory controller: breach triggers an out-of-memory kill
Block I/O controller: caps disk read and write speed
Union filesystem merges read-only layers; OverlayFS is the current standard driver
Copy-on-write duplicates a file only when it is modified

slides.visual_guidance: One cgroup boundary box with CPU/Memory/Disk meter icons, beside a layered stack merging into one view with a writable top layer.

sections.title: 2. Docker Architecture: Client, daemon, images, containers & registries; image vs container; layers & build caching

slides.heading: Docker Architecture Map

content.line: Docker runs as a client-server system: a command-line client talks to a background daemon that builds and runs containers using images pulled from a registry.
Docker client — CLI issuing commands like docker run
Docker daemon (dockerd) — service building and managing containers
Images — read-only templates stored locally or in a registry
Containers — running instances created from images
Registry — remote store such as Docker Hub for images

slides.visual_guidance: Diagram: client box with arrow to daemon box; daemon connects to an images store, a container box, and a registry cloud icon.

slides.heading: Docker Installation Steps

content.line: Docker installs differently per operating system, but every path ends with the same two verification commands before any practical work begins.

rows: Install VS Code; wsl --install; Docker Desktop (WSL 2 backend); open Docker Desktop
Install VS Code; Docker Desktop (Apple Silicon or Intel build); open Docker Desktop
Install VS Code; sudo apt install docker.io; sudo systemctl start docker

content.line: Line 1 — Displays the installed Docker CLI version.
Line 2 — Verifies that Docker can run a container; it typically pulls the image if needed and prints Hello from Docker!
Linux OS: If a Docker command fails due to permission issues, try running it with sudo, for example, sudo docker run hello-world.
Step 1 — Confirm WSL 2 Is Enabled (Windows)
PowerShell confirms WSL is installed/updated and the Virtual Machine Platform feature is Enabled — required before Docker Desktop will run on Windows
Step 2 — Choose Installation Options
Docker Desktop installer — Configuration screen, per-user installation with the WSL 2 backend
Step 3 — Installation Completes
Docker Desktop installer confirms “Installation succeeded”
Step 4 — Sign In Or Skip
First launch — Docker prompts to sign in or create a Docker Hub account; signing in is optional for local use and can be skipped
Step 5 — Redirected To The Desktop App
After sign-in (or skip), Docker redirects back to the desktop app
Step 6 — Confirm The Redirect
Windows asks permission to open Docker Desktop — confirms the handoff from browser back to the installed app
Step 7 — Docker Desktop Opens
Docker Desktop's Containers tab on first launch — empty, since nothing has been run yet
Step 8 — Verify From The Terminal
docker --version displays the installed Docker CLI version; docker run hello-world confirms the daemon pulled and ran an image — “Hello from Docker!” confirms success

slides.visual_guidance: See the 8-step screenshot walkthrough above — Windows install path shown end to end, from enabling WSL 2 through the docker run hello-world verification.

slides.heading: Image Vs Container

content.line: An image is a frozen, read-only template; a container is that template brought to life with its own writable layer on top.
Image: built once, never changes, stored by ID and tag
Container: created from an image, has a thin writable layer
One image can start many independent containers
Deleting a container never deletes its source image

slides.analogy: A cake recipe card is reused to bake many separate cakes — just as one Docker image can start many independent containers.
slides.visual_guidance: Side-by-side: image box with locked layers next to a container box showing the same layers plus a writable top layer.

slides.heading: Client Daemon Registry

content.line: Running an image that the daemon does not have locally triggers a pull from a registry — Docker Hub by default — before a container starts.
Explicit pull: docker pull nginx:alpine fetches an image with no container created — the same mechanism docker run triggers automatically
docker run hello-world: no flags — image name only, pulled if absent locally
Client sends the request over the daemon's local API socket
Daemon checks its local image cache first by name and tag
Pulled layers are cached, so a repeat run skips the registry

slides.visual_guidance: Arrow sequence: client -> daemon -> registry (dashed, only on cache miss) -> container created.

slides.heading: Part A Practical Steps

content.line: Part A works with an existing image, tracing every command from an explicit pull to removing a running web server container.
Step 1: docker pull nginx:alpine fetches the image explicitly, before any container runs
Step 2: docker images lists images already pulled
Step 3: docker run hello-world; expected Hello from Docker!
Step 4: docker ps shows currently running containers
Step 5: docker ps -a shows hello-world as Exited (0)
Step 6: docker run -d --name web-demo -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine starts a server
Step 7: docker ps confirms web-demo running with its port mapping
Step 8: browser at localhost:8080 shows Welcome to nginx!
Step 9: docker stop web-demo halts the container
Step 10: docker rm web-demo removes it; docker ps -a confirms it is gone

slides.visual_guidance: Numbered step strip 1 to 10, icons for terminal, container box, and browser window at the matching steps.

slides.heading: Container Lifecycle Commands

content.line: A long-running service container is started, mapped to a host port, then checked, stopped and removed through the client-daemon flow.
Nginx is used only to demonstrate a web application running inside a container, not as a production choice.
Line 1 — -d: run in background. --name web-demo: name the container. -p 8080:80: map host port 8080 to container port 80. nginx:alpine: the image used.
docker images: lists cached images before running
docker ps: expected web-demo Up, PORTS 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp
Browser at port 8080: expected the Welcome to nginx! page
docker stop web-demo: expected the container name echoed back
docker rm web-demo: expected web-demo absent from docker ps -a
Browser Check — Step 8
Browser at localhost:8080 — “Welcome to nginx!” confirms web-demo is serving traffic

slides.visual_guidance: Timeline strip: run -> ps -> browser -> stop -> rm, each step labelled with its command. Only the browser-result screenshot above is currently available.

slides.heading: Layers Build Caching

content.line: Each Dockerfile instruction adds one layer on top of the base image; a rebuild reuses an unchanged layer instead of redoing its work.
Line 1 — FROM sets the base layer.
Line 2 — COPY adds the HTML layer.
Line 3 — EXPOSE documents port 80, not published yet.
Cache key: instruction plus the files it touches
A changed instruction invalidates it and every layer after
Stable instructions first, frequently changing ones last

slides.analogy: Building a house floor by floor — if the foundation and lower floors remain unchanged, you don't rebuild them when making a change to the top floor, just as Docker reuses cached layers when earlier instructions remain unchanged.
slides.visual_guidance: Vertical stack of layer blocks labelled FROM, COPY, EXPOSE, with a cache tick mark on the unchanged ones.

slides.heading: Build Run Verify

content.line: Part B builds a custom image from a Dockerfile, confirming the same image-container relationship already seen with pulled images.
Lines 1-3 — A project folder holding the page content and the build instructions.

content.code: This web application is running inside a Docker container.

content.line: Lines 6-7 — The heading and paragraph this page serves, shown by the container once built and run.
Step 1: create folder cloud-docker-demo/ with index.html and Dockerfile
Step 2: write index.html with the page content above
Step 3: write Dockerfile with FROM, COPY and EXPOSE
Step 4: docker build -t cloud-docker-demo . builds the image
Step 5: docker images confirms cloud-docker-demo stored locally
Step 6: docker run -d --name cloud-web -p 8080:80 cloud-docker-demo starts it
Step 7: docker ps expected cloud-web with 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp
Step 8: browser at port 8080 expected the custom page
Step 9: docker stop cloud-web and docker rm cloud-web remove it
Step 10: docker images still lists cloud-docker-demo after removal
Step 1 — Project Folder Created
VS Code — cloud-docker-demo folder created in the file explorer
Step 2 — index.html Written
VS Code — index.html content: the custom page this container will serve
Step 3 — Dockerfile Written
VS Code — Dockerfile content: FROM, COPY and EXPOSE directives
Step 6 — Container Started
Terminal after docker run — cloud-web container ID printed
Step 7 — Port Mapping Confirmed
docker ps — cloud-web mapped to 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp

sections.title: 3. Containers vs VMs: Boot time, memory footprint, image size & density; isolation strength & security trade-offs

slides.heading: Four Comparison Dimensions

content.line: Containers and virtual machines isolate workloads differently, and that difference shows up in four measurable areas before any use case is chosen.
Boot time: how quickly each starts and becomes usable
Memory footprint: RAM consumed per workload at idle
Image size and density: how many instances fit per host
Isolation strength: kernel-level sharing versus hardware-level separation
Security trade-offs: what fails if the boundary is breached

slides.visual_guidance: Two stacks side by side: left hardware to hypervisor to guest OS to VMs; right hardware to host OS kernel to container engine to containers.

slides.heading: Boot Time And Memory

content.line: Starting a virtual machine boots a full guest operating system; starting a container launches one process on a kernel already running.

rows: Several hundred MB to a few GB (guest OS overhead)
A few MB to tens of MB (app plus runtime)

content.line: Cause: VM repeats bootloader, kernel init and service startup
Container skips straight to launching the application process
Lower per-instance memory lets more workloads run concurrently

slides.visual_guidance: Bar chart: boot time in seconds, VM bar far taller than container bar; second bar chart for idle memory, same proportion.

slides.heading: Image Size Density

content.line: Containers fit more workloads per host by sharing the host kernel and avoiding separate guest operating systems.

rows: Several GB (full guest OS plus app)
Tens of MB to a few hundred MB (app layers only)

content.line: Smaller images pull and deploy faster across a cluster
Higher density lowers infrastructure cost per workload on identical hardware
Shared base layers cut total storage across many container images

slides.visual_guidance: Grid diagram: one host square packed with few large VM blocks versus the same size host packed with many small container blocks.

slides.heading: Isolation Strength Compared

content.line: A virtual machine isolates at the hardware boundary with its own kernel; a container isolates at the process boundary on one shared kernel.
VM: separate guest kernel per instance, hypervisor enforces the boundary
Container: namespaces separate the view, cgroups cap the resources
Shared kernel means one kernel vulnerability can reach every container
VM: A guest OS crash usually does not affect sibling VMs.

slides.visual_guidance: Boundary diagram: VM boundary drawn around hardware layer (per guest); container boundary drawn around process layer (one shared kernel line beneath all).

slides.tr_title: Security Trade-offs Between Containers And VMs
slides.heading: Security Trade-offs

content.line: Stronger isolation does not mean fewer attacks; it changes how far a successful attack can spread once the boundary is crossed.
VM breakout may exploit a hypervisor vulnerability and can affect isolation between VMs
Container breakout exploits the shared kernel: mitigated by seccomp, SELinux, non-root users
Untrusted or multi-tenant code favours VM-grade isolation
Trusted internal services accept container isolation for speed and density

slides.visual_guidance: Two circles labelled blast radius: small circle around one VM after a breakout, large circle around the whole host after a container breakout.

sections.title: 4. Choosing Between Them: Container use cases; VM use cases; decision criteria

slides.heading: Choosing Between Them

content.line: Container and virtual machine strengths point to different workloads; matching the right one to the job is the real skill, not finding one universal winner.
Workload type: stateless microservices vs full-stack legacy apps
Isolation need: process-level sharing vs hardware-level separation
OS requirement: same kernel vs mixed operating systems
Scale and density: many light instances vs fewer, heavier ones

slides.visual_guidance: Diagram: a fork from one question mark — left arrow to a container icon tagged with workload types, right arrow to a VM icon tagged with workload types.

slides.heading: Container Use Cases

content.line: Containers suit workloads that restart often, scale horizontally, and ship as small, repeatable units — the opposite of a slow-booting, heavyweight guest.
Microservices: independently deployable services communicating over APIs
CI/CD pipelines: identical images carried from build to production
Cloud-native apps: run at scale on AWS ECS, EKS or Fargate
Stateless, short-lived tasks: batch jobs and queue workers
High-density hosting: many app instances packed onto one host

slides.visual_guidance: Row of icons: microservice mesh, CI/CD pipeline arrow, ECS/EKS logo, batch-job icon, stacked boxes for density.

slides.heading: VM Use Cases

content.line: Virtual machines earn their heavier footprint when a workload needs a full, isolated operating system or hardware access the host runtime cannot provide.
Legacy applications: tied to a specific OS version or kernel module
Mixed operating systems: Windows and Linux guests on one host
Strong multi-tenant isolation: separate kernels for untrusted workloads
Kernel-level or driver work: isolated environments for kernel development and driver testing.
Full-stack test labs: AWS EC2 instances cloning a production server exactly

slides.visual_guidance: Icons: Windows and Linux logos side by side, a lock for isolation, EC2 logo for the test-lab case.

slides.heading: Decision Criteria Map

content.line: No single criterion decides the choice; the table weighs isolation, OS diversity, density and workload lifetime side by side.

rows: Multiple OS types on one host
Full OS control or legacy environment requirements

content.line: Production systems often combine both — containers scheduled onto VM-based hosts — using the VM as the security boundary and containers for density within it.

slides.visual_guidance: Keep the table as the slide centrepiece; below it, a small nested box showing container icons inside one VM icon to depict the hybrid pattern.

sections.title: 5. Tooling & Registries: VirtualBox, KVM, Hyper-V & VMware; Docker, Podman & containerd; public vs private registries; tagging strategy

slides.heading: Tooling Landscape

content.line: Running virtual machines or containers in production means picking a hypervisor or engine, then a registry to distribute the resulting images.
Virtualization tools: VirtualBox, KVM, Hyper-V, VMware
Container engines: Docker, Podman, containerd
Registries: public vs private
Tagging: naming scheme for image versions

slides.visual_guidance: Two-column diagram: VM tools column, container tools column, both arrows pointing down into one shared Registry box.

slides.tr_title: Comparing VirtualBox, KVM, Hyper-V And VMware
slides.heading: VM Tooling Compared

content.line: Each virtualization product fits a different deployment, from a laptop test lab to a production data centre.

rows:
AWS Nitro, Google Cloud,
OpenStack clouds

slides.visual_guidance: Four-row table, one small vendor logo icon beside each tool name.

slides.heading: Beneath Docker's Daemon

content.line: Docker delegates container execution to containerd. Kubernetes can use containerd through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), without relying on Docker Engine.
containerd: split out of Docker in 2016, now a separate project
containerd runs the OCI Runtime Spec through runc underneath
Podman removes the central daemon altogether; each container is a direct process
Podman's rootless mode starts containers without any root privilege

slides.analogy: A city bus needs a central depot dispatching every trip, while an auto-rickshaw driver picks up a passenger directly with no depot involved — exactly as Podman starts a container directly, with no daemon standing between the command and the running process.
slides.visual_guidance: Diagram: Docker box with arrow down to containerd box; separate Podman box with no daemon, arrow straight to container.

slides.heading: Engines Compared

content.line: The three tools sit at different layers of one stack, and that layering decides which one fits a given deployment.

rows: Yes, when run as a normal user
Minimal (ctr, for debugging); nerdctl for Docker-like use

slides.visual_guidance: Four-row comparison table, highlight the Primary Role row in a contrasting colour.

slides.heading: Public Vs Private

content.line: A registry stores and distributes container images; which kind is used decides who is able to pull a given image.
Public registry: Docker Hub, where public images can generally be pulled by anyone
Private registry: Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry
Self-hosted option: Harbor, run inside an organisation's own network
Chosen for security, compliance or protecting proprietary images

slides.analogy: A public registry is like a library open to any visitor, while a private registry is like an office cupboard that opens only with an employee's key — exactly as a private registry demands authentication before an image can be pulled.
slides.visual_guidance: Split diagram: public registry with an open padlock icon, private registry with a closed padlock, both feeding a docker pull arrow.

slides.heading: Tagging Strategy

content.line: Image tags provide human-readable names for versions, while digests identify exact image content for reliable redeployment.
Semantic versioning: major.minor.patch, for example app:2.3.1
latest tag: moves with every push, unsafe for production rollback
Immutable tag: git-commit hash, for example app:a1b2c3d, never overwritten
Environment tags: app:staging, app:prod mark the pipeline stage

slides.visual_guidance: Timeline of three pushes to one repository, each landing a different immutable tag, with the latest pointer jumping between them.
